catalog_quote: Fivaz states the following in the introduction to his Reference Grammar of Oshindonga: “Ndonga, like all the other southern Bantu languages is a tone language, which is to say that the pitches on an utterance play a significant part in contrasts between lexical forms as well as in grammatical signalling. It is impossible to conceive of a comprehensive reference grammar of this language in which tone is not treated. However, having said this, it should be observed that the interpretation of the clearly audible pitches of the language in terms of a system is a complex matter. This description is in this important respect, no less than in any other, exploratory in nature. But, the tonal system in particular calls for more careful investigation than was possible in the time available for this study.” (Fivaz 1986:xix)

new_statements.rule_in_words: The primary grammar (Fivaz 1986) is reported to say only that Ndonga is a tone language in which pitch distinguishes lexical forms; no opened source says where word stress falls in Ndonga, and nothing found says whether there is penultimate prominence or lengthening.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None. Halme adds that Fivaz marks tone 'and discusses it to some extent', giving 'a number of (sometimes contradictory)' [statements], and that 'a detailed account of Ndonga tone is still lacking'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical tone ('contrasts between lexical forms'); the bracketed gap in the quote is text between two verified fragments that the snippet API did not return, and the closing words come from the same Fivaz 1986:xix quotation as cited by Halme. Halme's own penultimate-accent remark concerns Brincker/Tönjes on Kwanyama, not Ndonga.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources concern Oshindonga, the standardized Ndonga written variety of Oshiwambo (ndon1254, ISO ndo); Glottolog dialects Kwaludhi (kwal1254) and Eunda-Kolonkadhi (eund1238) are not separately described. Halme 2004 is a grammar of the sister language Kwanyama (kuan1247) and only reports on Ndonga second-hand; Brincker 1891's 'Oshindonga' column is 19th-century Ndonga. Hamakali & Mbenzi 2016 treats Oshikwanyama, and the Uushona papers treat 'Oshiwambo' generically.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Ndonga has an empty rule, and the only existing statement (Fivaz 1986:xix via Halme 2004) says Ndonga is a tone language and gives no stress placement. Seidel 1892 adds a placement claim: word accent usually on the first stem syllable. This does not contradict the tonal characterisation (Fivaz, as quoted, does not deny stress and Seidel does not discuss tone), so it is compatible added detail rather than a conflicting placement; note it is a different descriptive type (accentual, stem-initial) from an 1892 compiler who worked from Finnish mission Bible translations (Einleitung, pp. 129-130) and who uses the identical formula for Herero in Part II.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word accent (Wortton) falls as a rule on the stem-initial (root-initial) syllable, i.e. the first syllable after the prefixes: o-ma-tú-li-lo from the verb root tula. Hedged with 'gewöhnlich' (usually). Nothing is said about tone for Oshindonga; vowels are described as mostly short with marked length (item 3). The same pronunciation section (items 1-5) covers letters, vowel length, elision and diphthongs; item 6 is the only prosodic statement in the Oshindonga part (pp. 127-180).
new_statements.exceptions: Only the hedge 'gewöhnlich' (usually); no exceptions are listed for Oshindonga (unlike the Herero part of the same book, p. II Lautlehre item 3, which says deviations from stem-initial Wortton are marked with a written acute accent).
new_statements.identity_note: Seidel 1892 Part III explicitly describes Oshindonga, 'der Dialekt des Ondonga-Stammes' of the Ovambo (Einleitung p. 129), i.e. Ndonga proper (ndon1254), based on the orthography and translations of the Finnish mission (Rautanen, Reijonen); Parts I and II of the same volume are Nama and Herero and were not used for this item.

readall_conflicts: No direct contradiction. The modern reference description (Fivaz 1986:xix, known only second-hand through Halme 2004) characterises Ndonga as a tone language and states no stress rule; Seidel 1892 (p. 131) states that the word accent usually lies on the first stem syllable (omatúlilo < tula) and says nothing about tone. The two are compatible (stem-initial prominence in a tonal Bantu language), but they are different kinds of statement: Seidel's is a 19th-century compiler's 'Wortton' formula, identical to the one he gives for Herero in the same volume, hedged with 'gewöhnlich' and unsupported by further examples, so it should be recorded as an early stem-initial accent claim of low-to-medium authority rather than as an established stress rule.
